title: The hypertrophy series: overspeed eccentrics vs regular negatives
summary: NH compares controlled negatives with overspeed eccentrics, rejecting the idea that negative speed does not matter and dismissing raw fast negatives as injury-prone. Band-assisted overspeed eccentrics are fine if the lifter actively resists the band on the way down; negatives should be fluid and controlled, neither exaggeratedly slow nor rushed.
claims: He favors slow negatives, but speed matters: the claim that negative speed is irrelevant because the distance is the same ignores time under tension
A lengthened muscle under load accumulates muscle damage over time, as shown by benefits from a static stretched hold like heavy shrug holds stretching the traps
Time under tension is relevant but too chaotic to be a main programming principle
Exaggerated 3-4 second negatives are counterproductive: unnatural, poor for power production, and they limit the strength progression hypertrophy relies on
Fast unloaded negatives meant to lengthen the muscle faster are hogwash; the load pulling on the muscle matters, and rushing risks injury and a botched reversal at the bottom
Bands add tension at lockout and less at the chest on bench, matching the strength curve; he does not use them but has no issue with them
Slamming the bar down with bands and bouncing it gives no extra hypertrophy benefit
A negative means actively resisting gravity, rearranging the body around the bar to keep technique stable and arrive at the bottom in perfect position to press back up
Lifters who resist the bands on the negative do get somewhat more hypertrophic benefit; not major per rep, but worthwhile when programmed over time
Negatives should be natural, fluid and controlled with some speed; never resist for 10 seconds or let the weight fall
Hypertrophy, like life, is a game of balance: negatives that are too slow and too fast both belong in the garbage
